unit.unitTitle: The Body, Illness and the Clinic
unit.unitOverview: When you are ill is the worst possible time to be searching for words, and it is exactly when you most need them. This unit gives you the three sentence frames English uses for saying what is wrong, the word for giving and understanding advice, and the skill of reading a medicine label. It is short on grammar and long on things you will say word for word, because that is what this situation calls for.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. There are only three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 is three frames to learn by heart, not a rule to work out.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a medicine label — read it twice.
Do the Practice. Practice 6 asks you to prepare for a real appointment.
Record yourself describing three different problems.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is shorter on grammar than the others, and that is deliberate. When you are ill you do not want to be building sentences. You want three or four things you can say without thinking.
So learn these by heart.
The first pattern is how English says what is wrong, and there are three frames. You need all three because they take different kinds of word.
The first: I have got a, plus the name of the problem. I have got a headache. I have got a cough. I have got a temperature. Notice these problems are things you HAVE — English treats them as objects you are carrying.
The second: my, plus the body part, plus hurts. My back hurts. My throat hurts. My tooth hurts. Use this when the problem is a place on your body rather than a named illness.
And for more than one place, hurts becomes hurt. My legs hurt. That is the ordinary s rule you already know from Unit 3.
The third: I feel, plus a word for how you are. I feel ill. I feel tired. I feel sick. I feel better.
Be careful with one of those. In many kinds of English, I feel sick means I am about to vomit, not I am unwell in general. If you mean generally unwell, say I feel ill or I am not well.
So: I have got a for a named problem, my something hurts for a place, and I feel for a general state. Three frames. Learn them the way you learned the four help phrases in Unit 3, until they arrive without assembly.
Second pattern: should. This is the word for advice.
You should rest. You should drink water. You should see a doctor.
And the negative: you should not lift anything heavy. You shouldn't drive.
Should behaves exactly like can, which you learned in Unit 3. It never changes — I should, she should, never she shoulds. It needs no do in the question: should I come back? And the verb after it takes no to: you should rest, never you should to rest.
That is three rules you already know, applied to a new word. If you can use can, you can use should.
One difference from can is worth knowing. Should is advice, not obligation. It says this is a good idea. It does not say you have no choice. The words for no choice come later in the course.
Third pattern is not grammar at all. It is reading a medicine label, and it is here because the information on one is arranged in a fixed way and once you know the shape you can read any of them.
A label tells you four things. How much to take. How often. When to stop, or how long. And what not to do while taking it.
That fourth part is where the important information usually hides, and it is usually written as a negative instruction, which you learned to read in Unit 6. Do not take more than. Do not take with. Do not give to children under.
One serious point before we go on. This course is not medical advice, and the label in this unit is a practice document for a medicine that does not exist. Never take anything on the basis of an exercise. If you are ill, ask a pharmacist or a doctor — and this unit gives you the words to do that.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: Write It Down Before You Go
readings.passageScript:
An appointment is short. Ten minutes, often less. And it happens at the one moment when your English is at its worst, because you are ill and worried and the room is unfamiliar.
So do the language part before you go, when you are calm and have a dictionary.
Write down four things.
What is wrong. One sentence, using one of the three frames. My back hurts. I have got a cough. I feel tired all the time.
When it started. A date or a length of time. Since Monday. For three weeks. On the fourteenth.
What makes it better or worse. This is the question you will be asked and it is the one nobody prepares for. It is worse in the morning. It hurts when I lift things. It is better when I rest.
What you want to ask. Two questions, no more. Is it serious? How long will it take?
Take the paper in with you. Nobody minds. Show it if speaking is hard — a doctor would far rather read four clear lines than watch somebody struggle.
And take your medicines with you, or a photograph of the boxes. You will be asked what you are taking, and the names are hard to say and easy to get wrong.

readings.title: Who to Ask, and When
readings.passageScript:
Not every problem needs a doctor, and knowing where to go saves days of waiting.
A chemist can advise you about small things without an appointment and without payment for the advice. Coughs, colds, small pains, skin problems, and whether two medicines can be taken together. This is what a chemist is trained for and it is not a lesser service — they are the fastest correct answer for a great many problems.
A doctor is for things that do not get better, things that keep coming back, anything you are worried about, and anything that needs a prescription.
An emergency service is for things that are dangerous now. Difficulty breathing, chest pain, heavy bleeding, someone who cannot be woken.
Here is the practical part. When you telephone a surgery for an appointment, you will be asked what it is about. Many people find this uncomfortable and answer vaguely. Do not. The person asking is deciding how soon you are seen, and a vague answer gets a later appointment.
Say it plainly: I have got chest pain. I have had a cough for three weeks. My child has a temperature.
And one thing worth knowing in any country: if you are told to wait and you become worse while waiting, that is a new situation. Telephone again and say what has changed.

grammar.title: Three ways to say what is wrong
grammar.explanation: This is not a rule to work out. It is three sentence frames to learn by heart, because you will need them at the moment when working anything out is hardest.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
1. A NAMED problem → I have got a …
     I have got a headache.
     I have got a cough.
     I have got a temperature.

2. A PLACE on your body → my … hurts
     My back hurts.
     My throat hurts.
     (more than one place: my legs hurt)

3. A GENERAL feeling → I feel …
     I feel ill.  I feel tired.  I feel better.
grammar.workedExample:
Your throat is painful. Which frame?
1. Is it a named problem with its own word? There is one — a sore throat. So frame 1 works: I have got a sore throat.
2. Is it a place on your body? Yes, the throat. So frame 2 also works: My throat hurts.
3. Both are correct, and people use both.
Now try: you are generally unwell with no particular place. Frames 1 and 2 have nothing to attach to, so you need frame 3: I feel ill.
That is how to choose — see which frame has something to hold on to.
grammar.commonMistake: The trap is I feel sick. In many kinds of English that means you are about to vomit, not that you are generally unwell. If you mean unwell, say I feel ill or I am not well. This misunderstanding is common and occasionally serious.
grammar.memoryTip: Named problem, place, or general feeling — one frame each.

grammar.title: Should: giving advice
grammar.explanation: Should is the word for advice. It behaves exactly like can, which you learned in Unit 3 — so if you can use one, you already know how to use the other.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
You should rest.

Negative: You should not lift anything heavy.
          (short form: shouldn't)
Question: Should I come back?

Never changes:  she should, not she shoulds
No do:          should I come back, not do I should
No to after it: you should rest, not you should to rest

2. Put the person first: You…
3. Add should: You should…
4. Add the verb, plain, with no to: You should rest for a few days.

For the question, move should to the front: Should I rest for a few days? Nothing else changes — the same three rules as can.

grammar.title: Reading a medicine label
grammar.explanation: A label is arranged in a fixed order, and once you know the shape you can read any of them. It answers four questions, and the fourth is where the important information usually hides.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
1. HOW MUCH  — the dose
     1 or 2 tablets

2. HOW OFTEN — the interval
     every 4 to 6 hours

3. THE LIMIT — how much in a day, or for how long
     not more than 8 in 24 hours
     not for more than 3 days

4. WHAT NOT TO DO — the warnings
     Do not take with …
     Do not give to children under …
grammar.workedExample:
A label says: 1 or 2 tablets every 4 to 6 hours. Do not take more than 8 tablets in 24 hours.
You take 2 at a time. How many doses can you have in a day?
1. The limit is 8 tablets.
2. Your dose is 2 tablets.
3. 8 divided by 2 is 4.
So four doses.
4. Now check it against the interval: 4 doses, at least 4 hours apart, is at least 16 hours. That fits in a day.
The label gave you the limit in tablets, not in doses. Working out the doses is the step that prevents taking too many.
grammar.commonMistake: The commonest error is reading the first dose block and stopping. Labels usually have more than one — adults, older children, young children — and the numbers differ. Find the block that describes the person taking it, and read that one.
grammar.memoryTip: Find the block for the right person. Then read the limit as well as the dose.

1. One or two tablets  2. Every four to six hours  3. Eight tablets in twenty-four hours  4. One tablet every six hours, maximum four in twenty-four hours  5. Three days  6. Do not take it with another medicine containing paralex; do not drink alcohol; do not chew the tablets. (Any two.)

activities.title: Practice 4 — Work out the doses
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Use the label in Reading 3. Show your working.
1. An adult takes two tablets at a time. How many doses may they have in 24 hours?
2. An adult takes one tablet at a time. How many doses may they have in 24 hours?
3. A 15-year-old takes the correct dose. How many doses in 24 hours?
4. If an adult takes two tablets every four hours for a whole day, how many would that be? Is it allowed?

activities.answerSummary:
1. Eight divided by two is four doses.
2. Eight doses — but check the interval: eight doses at least four hours apart needs at least 32 hours, so eight is not possible in 24. Six is the realistic maximum.
3. Four doses, one tablet each, six hours apart — that is exactly 24 hours.
4. Every four hours for 24 hours is six doses, which at two tablets each is twelve tablets. That is NOT allowed — the limit is eight.
5. Six tablets a day, 24 in the box, so four days. But the label says do not take it for more than three days without speaking to a doctor, so the box holds more than you should take alone.
Numbers 2, 4 and 5 all show the same thing: the dose, the interval and the limit have to be read together, and each one alone gives the wrong answer.

1. My head hurts. (frame 2) — or I have got a headache (frame 1). Both correct.
2. I have got a cough. (frame 1)
3. I feel ill. (frame 3)
4. My legs hurt. (frame 2 — note hurt, not hurts, because legs is plural)

1. You should see a doctor. (no to)
2. She should rest. (no s)
3. Should I come back? (no do — move should to the front)

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. Eight divided by two is four doses.
2. Eight doses — but check the interval: eight doses at least four hours apart needs at least 32 hours, so eight is not possible in 24. Six is the realistic maximum.
3. Four doses, one tablet each, six hours apart — that is exactly 24 hours.
4. Every four hours for 24 hours is six doses, which at two tablets each is twelve tablets. That is NOT allowed — the limit is eight.
5. Six tablets a day, 24 in the box, so four days. But the label says do not take it for more than three days without speaking to a doctor, so the box holds more than you should take alone.
Numbers 2, 4 and 5 all show the same thing: the dose, the interval and the limit have to be read together, and each one alone gives the wrong answer.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. CHEMIST  2. DOCTOR  3. EMERGENCY  4. CHEMIST  5. DOCTOR  6. CHEMIST  7. EMERGENCY  8. DOCTOR (you need a prescription, though the chemist may be able to advise on the process)
The pattern behind it: a chemist for small things and for questions about medicines; a doctor for anything that lasts, repeats, worries you, or needs a prescription; emergency for anything dangerous now.
Compare 1 and 2. The same symptom becomes a different answer once it has lasted three weeks — that is the thing to notice.
